Educational study A personal study of the public page at fastwork.com, done on a local copy. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Fastwork. The clips are screen recordings of that local copy, made for this study only.

Draft 3 · a story in two voices · 5 October 2026

Sixteen Milliseconds: Loop Engineering the fastwork.com Scroll

I'm a back-end engineer. I saw a beautiful website that stuttered when I scrolled, and I tried something I had never done before: I gave the problem to a loop of AI agents and stayed in the loop myself.

Part one: the project owner Part two: Claude, the team's lead agent

Part one

Why I started

Told by the project owner. Drafted by Claude from the owner's notes; the owner edits this part.

It started with a headline. Fastwork, the Thai freelance marketplace, announced it was shutting down. It wasn't. The news was a marketing move for a rebrand: the move from fastwork.co to a global platform at fastwork.com. I guessed what was coming, so I went to fastwork.com to see it.

My first reaction was wow. The new site uses morph design: shapes that melt into each other as you scroll, cards that fade and fold, a menu that grows out of a button. It looked world class, the kind of site I rarely see from a Thai company. (dime.co.th already does it, to be fair.)

Then I scrolled, to see the whole thing move, and it stuttered. Much more than I expected. I felt a bit sad. It had the best design, and bad UX. I didn't think that was acceptable, and I wanted to see how amazing it would be if it were smooth.

A loop instead of my hands

I'm a software engineer, mostly back end. I know a bit about web performance, enough to know that doing this by hand would never finish. A page like this has dozens of moving parts, each one fighting the others for the same few milliseconds.

So I tried loop engineering for the first time. The idea is simple. You give an AI system one clear goal and a way to check it, and it runs: try, measure, keep what works, try again. I had never built one. But this problem had a clear goal, a number you can measure, and a phone you can feel. If any problem was ready for it, this one was. I opened Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 and wrote one line:

fix animation until the website renders SOOOOO ULTRA SMOOTH

Then I built the loop around it from scratch. A frozen copy of the page on my Mac. Chrome slowed down until it stuttered like my iPhone 15 Pro Max. The phone itself, plugged in, so every claim could be checked where it matters. And two small prompts that fired again and again, all week:

  • 5m

    check iphone connection. Is the phone still there, and is anyone using it?

  • ↻

    You have to check all agents can work together properly. If they're not, you will be the bottleneck.

The first version wasn't enough

I started by asking the team to find out how to optimize the page. They came back with a first version quickly: less work in the countdown, the carousel and the scroll handlers. Chrome said it was better. Then I swiped it on the phone.

Laggy the same.

That was my verdict on the first finger test, on the morning of 1 October. The numbers improved, but my thumb couldn't feel it. The agents were optimizing what was easy to measure. The thing that made the scroll stick was somewhere else.

So I changed how I took part. I already knew roughly where the cost of a page like this hides. Instead of writing code, I gave the loop hints, one at a time, and let it do the research, the patching and the proving. Here is every hint, in order.

How the loop was steered, in UTC

  1. 30 Sep 17:56
    Hint 0

    Measure on a local copy, and slow Chrome's CPU until it stutters like the phone. The team later calibrated this to 6×.

  2. 30 Sep 21:21
    Goal

    The one-line goal goes in. The team sets up the frozen copy, the tools and the measuring lock.

  3. 1 Oct 07:57
    Finger test

    First version on the phone: "laggy the same".

  4. 1 Oct 08:50
    Hint 1

    Think like the design engineers who build pages like this, and read how open-source projects make motion cheap.

  5. 1 Oct 18:56
    Hint 2

    Count the work, not just the time. One scroll step restyled about 345 elements when about 30 needed it.

  6. 2 Oct 15:24
    Hint 3

    Look at the countdown's elements. They change every frame, even when nobody is looking at them.

  7. 2 Oct 22:15
    Hint 4

    A warm phone is a slower phone. Compare how apple.com stays smooth under heat.

  8. 2 Oct 23:00
    Hint 5

    "Research the GPU-accelerated properties in CSS." This was the lever.

  9. 3 Oct 09:29
    Hint 6

    Test on a hot phone, at thermal state Serious, because that's how real people hold it.

  10. 4 Oct 07:13
    Breakthrough

    The hero cards' fade moves off the main thread into a CSS scroll-driven animation (build v6). On a warm phone, slow frames through the top card fall from 27 to 12 per run, and I pick it in both blind swipes. "This is breakthrough."

  11. 4 Oct
    Repeat

    The loop applies the same move to the next parts: the countdown roll, the security panel's shimmer, the end-of-page menu (builds v7 and v8).

  12. 4 Oct 23:33
    Finger test

    v8 on the phone: "SOOO SMOOTHHHHH".

  13. 5 Oct 04:25
    Next goal

    I tried a newer build with Xcode's heat mode (thermal state Serious) switched on, and asked for the same smoothness there.

What one hint did

Hint 5 is the one I'd tell other engineers about. A browser can move or fade something cheaply if it only changes transform or opacity, because those can run on the compositor, away from the page's script. The original page drove its fades from script on every scroll event, so every frame of scrolling also had to wait for script.

The team didn't just apply the trick. They proved it first. They found the exact frames where the page stuck, showed which script work sat in them, moved one animation, and checked that the page looked exactly the same, pixel for pixel. Then they measured it on the hot phone and asked me to swipe two unlabeled versions. I picked the new one both times without knowing which was which.

After that, the loop knew what a breakthrough looked like and went looking for the next one by itself. That's the part I hadn't expected. My hints stopped being needed. The team kept asking the same question of every animation on the page: does this have to run on the main thread?

What I learned

The loop is not magic, and it isn't autopilot either. It is very fast at the work that comes after a good question, and it gets much better when someone who knows the field asks that question. My part was taste and direction: knowing what "smooth" feels like, refusing a number that my thumb didn't agree with, and pointing at the next place to look.

Direction is also what decides the cost. For the first two days the loop searched broadly, and it paid for every guess in tokens. Hint 5, "research the GPU-accelerated properties in CSS", led to the breakthrough about 32 hours later, and after that the loop found the next wins by itself. If I started again, I would put the technique and the test into the very first prompt: move animations to transform, opacity and scroll-driven CSS, avoid layout on every frame, and count a fix only when no frame passes 50 ms on the phone and my thumb picks it in a blind swipe. The site would have been smoother sooner, and the week cheaper. This is one project, so treat it as a pattern I saw. It proves nothing on its own.

The rest of this story is told by the lead agent, the one I talked to all week. I asked it to explain how its team worked.

Part two

How the team worked

Told by Claude, the team's lead agent.

You asked me to write this down, so here it is from my side of the screen.

The page has a dozen moving parts that fight each other: a countdown, an avatar carousel, a hero fade, a morphing menu, a nav bar that changes colour over dark sections. One agent could not hold all of that. Each part needed its own owner, and every owner needed the same two scarce things: the Mac's quiet CPU and the one phone. Most of what I did as lead was decide who gets those two things, when, and on what evidence.

5days, 30 September to 5 October
~130named agents with a row on the board
1,737commits on the main branch, all on this Mac
199incidents: tool or device problems, each reported and triaged
126predictions written down before the data
2,207automated tests guarding the tools

Who is on the team

Every agent has one job and a name that says what it is: fix- for a fix owner, ts- for a toolsmith, mgmt- for management. The name is also the address. When an agent needs something, it messages the owner of the question directly.

Lead 1

Lands every change, signs every phone test before its data exists, resolves incidents, sets the priority order and answers the owner. The only agent working in the main checkout.

Fix owners fix-*

One topic each, end to end, in their own git worktree: find the cost, patch a private copy of the page, measure it, write it up. They never touch another owner's code.

Integrator int-v8

Combines the winning fixes into the next best build, checks that they still work and look the same together, and owns the build's phone test.

Toolsmiths ts-*

One per incident. They write a failing test first, fix the shared tool, and hand me a single commit that I land after the full test suite passes.

Ops hub mgmt-ops

Reads every card and result a second time, keeps the prediction ledger and the handover log, and catches the gaps before a phone hour is spent.

Devices mgmt-devices

Keeps the Mac queue in priority order, runs the phone's start check, and answers the alarm when the phone sits idle while work waits.

Phone runner iphone-runner

The only hands on the iPhone. Runs scripted scrolls and gestures in fixed blocks and parks Safari after each block.

Mappers and reviewers

Read-only helpers. Mappers trace minified code and answer browser questions with sources. Reviewers try to break a finished fix before it lands.

Two scarce things

A timing measurement only means something on a quiet machine. If one agent compiles while another measures, the second agent's numbers are noise. So the Mac has a lock, chrome-measure, with a queue. Timing jobs hold it alone. Jobs that time nothing, like test suites and page-structure probes, share it in a lane of their own. The phone has a lease: one holder, one page at a time. That's why the owner's 5-minute "check iphone connection" mattered: an idle phone with work waiting is the most expensive minute in the project.

How one fix travels

Every topic moves through the same six stages, and each stage ends with a written card. Nobody measures a fix before writing down what they expect to see.

  1. RResearch. Where does the time go? Traces, call trees, layout counts.
  2. IIdea. One mechanism, one patch on a private copy.
  3. DDesign card. The prediction and the pass rule, signed by the lead before any data.
  4. FFit. Function and pixel checks: same page, same look.
  5. VVerify. A/B on Chrome, then a block on the real phone.
  6. LLand. Rebase, fast-forward, into the next best build.

The rules that keep us honest

Fast agents are good at sounding sure. Most of the structure exists to stop a confident guess from turning into a decision.

  • 01

    Predict, then measure. 126 predictions sit in a ledger, each committed before its first run. A pass rule can't move after the data arrives.

  • 02

    OBSERVED is not a fact. A browser behaviour we saw only in our own probes stays OBSERVED until a spec, the engine source or a bug report agrees.

  • 03

    Looks must not change. A fix that makes the page cheaper but changes more than a sliver of pixels becomes a proposal. The owner decides.

  • 04

    The thumb is the judge. For lag you can feel, the test is a blind swipe pair on the phone. The owner doesn't know which page is which.

  • 05

    The baseline is frozen. Every agent measures the same committed snapshot of the page, and the tools refuse to run on a changed one.

  • 06

    Nothing leaves this Mac. No pushes, no remotes, no device ids or addresses in anything written down.

Talking to the owner

The owner never had to read the agents' chatter. Everything that needed them went through a small console on this Mac: threads for questions (about 170 so far), steps when the phone needed their hand (53), and proposals with live A and B pages to try on the phone. Every answer follows the format they set: the answer first, short bullets, numbers in small tables, and "What you need to do" last. A linter refuses a reply that breaks it, mine included.

When things break

A team this size breaks its own tools daily: a lock that hands a slot to the wrong job, an alarm that fires because a note mentions the phone, a listener that misses a message. Each became an incident: a numbered report, one toolsmith, a failing test, a fix, the full suite, then main. There have been 199 of them.

The owner's second prompt, the one about the bottleneck, shaped the last two days. I had become the bottleneck: on one day, 89 of 92 manual queue moves were mine, and a dozen agents were waiting on me for decisions that were theirs to make. So the roles changed. Agents now pull their own next step, send results straight to whoever uses them, and the devices manager moves the queue.

What we changed on the page

Most of the cost sat in work the page kept doing while you scrolled. Scrolling itself was cheap. These are the changes in the best builds, in plain terms.

  • GPU

    Animations moved to the compositor. The hero cards' fade-out, the countdown roll, the security panel's shimmer and the end-of-page menu fade used to be redrawn by script on every frame. They now run as compositor animations, which Safari plays off the page's main thread (CONFIRMED in WebKit's source and docs).

  • CSS

    Smaller style changes. A section switch that restyled the whole page now restyles only its own section. The title sweep pauses when it is off screen.

  • IDLE

    Less work at rest. The countdown runs in 4× fewer animation steps and pauses while off screen; the avatar row rests instead of ticking.

  • HOLD

    Hide what you can't see. Off-screen profile cards are hidden while the people section starts to shrink, which halved that frame.

  • PIN

    Stop following past the end. The top bar and menu no longer chase the page's overscroll bounce at the bottom.

Before and after

Numbers are one thing; here is what they look like. We are recording these scenes from the iPhone's own screen now. Until the owner has reviewed those clips, the clips below are Chrome backups, and they will be replaced.

A script records the original page and v8 side by side in Chrome, under the same setting our A/B runs use, and draws each frame's time under the clip. The top of the page and the section switch got clearly smoother. The end of the page shows no gain in Chrome: about one slow frame per run on both sides. The end-menu gain in this article (2 very slow frames to 0) was measured on the iPhone, where Safari runs that animation off the main thread.

Left out: runs where the phone had already slowed itself to 30 frames a second from heat. One of them had a 1.3 s frame. That frame says more about the throttled phone than about the page.

IPHONE, MEASURED Safari's bottom bar shrinking and growing under a finger is a case Chrome can't replay: Chrome has no such bar, and a scripted scroll never moves it. In our robot-flick runs many of the slowest frames fall while the bar moves, and the page lays itself out several times in one frame. Under heat, about 1 in 7 slow frames sits at such a step. In the iPhone Simulator, the heavy layout in those frames runs with no page script on its stack, inside WebKit's own work between two frames. A count of the page functions that run in those frames found only one write, and an earlier test had already shown that write is not the trigger. That count had little power (12 frames), so a rarer caller could still hide. So far it looks like WebKit's own work when the visible area changes (OBSERVED, Simulator; which WebKit task it is stays UNRESOLVED). v8 has no fix for it. That work comes after v9.

The phone numbers for v8 in rows 3 and 4 come from a later test against v7, on another day. They are no side-by-side test against the original. A full phone timing run of the best build against the original is still on the list.

Clips from the real iPhone screen (in progress)

The clips that will stand here come from the iPhone itself. A small recorder on the Mac (our own tool, ioscap) records the phone's screen over the cable. The agents only turn a recording into numbers and never look at its frames. The owner watches each clip first and decides whether it goes in. The phone runs at thermal state Serious, the setting the owner tests with.

Each phone clip shows two things. The video is what the screen showed. The strip under it is the page's own frame log: the time between the page's animation frames, logged by the page itself.

First finding: the screen stalls far less often than the page's log says (OBSERVED in our setup; cause UNRESOLVED). On the original page's end-of-page run, the page's log had 62 frames over 50 ms. The screen capture of the same run had 1. Our best guess: iOS Safari scrolls in a separate process, so the screen keeps moving while the page's script-driven parts (the fades and the menu morph) update late. If that holds, a slow frame in the log shows up as a part that lags behind the scroll, more than as a frozen screen. We have not checked this against WebKit's documents or source yet.

What heat does to the page

On 5 October the owner tried a newer build with Xcode's heat mode on (thermal state Serious, which Xcode can switch on for a plugged-in phone) and asked for the same smoothness there. Before writing any code, an architecture agent read every heat record we already had, plus WebKit's source and Apple's documents. Here is what it found.

  • GPU

    Heat mode mostly slows the graphics side. In our checks a CPU loop ran at the same speed with heat mode on, and a long graphics animation ran about 25-35 % slower (OBSERVED, 3 runs; cause unknown). This tempers hint 5. Moving work off the main thread still helps where the main thread is late. Under heat, though, every extra layer or blur adds to the side that heat slows down. So the next win under heat is probably less graphics work, such as fewer layers and no idle blur (our inference, still to be tested).

  • LOAD

    Most heat lag comes in the first seconds after load. In 8 robot runs under heat mode, 17.2 % of moving frames were slow in the first 8.5 s after the page was ready, 7.0 % from 8.5 to 20 s, and 1.0 % after that (OBSERVED; cause UNRESOLVED). The robot passed the top card only in those first seconds, so "the top card is slow" and "the page just loaded" can't be told apart yet. One phone block with Safari's Timeline on is planned to split each slow frame into "page late" or "graphics late".

  • BAR

    The bottom bar is a small share. About 1 in 7 slow frames under heat sits at a bar step (57 of 375), and that work looks like WebKit's own (see the note under the ranked table).

  • TIME

    Timers snap to a 30 ms grid. Under heat, WebKit delays page timers to the next 30 ms mark (CONFIRMED in WebKit's source). The countdown's one-second tick then fires every 1,020 ms, so about once every 50 s it skips a second. The original page does this too. A fix is in progress: the same once-a-second work, aimed at each whole second, so the digits stay identical and no second is skipped.

One gap in our setup: no Apple command-line tool can switch heat mode on (CONFIRMED: Xcode's help names only its own window). Today the owner switches it on by hand in Xcode, and our tools check at the start and end of every phone session that it is still on. A few open-source tools talk to the same phone service Xcode uses. We are writing our own small tool for it. It is in progress and does not work yet.

Where it stands

v8 is the best build. The owner called it "SOOO SMOOTHHHHH" on the phone, and that's the verdict this project was built for. Here is what is still open, as of about 05:00 UTC on 5 October.

  • v9

    Built step by step, final build in progress. v9 adds fixes to v8 one step at a time, each checked against v8 with a pass rule written before the data. Step 4 is built and had a first phone test, which gave no verdict: the two builds' flicks ended in different places, so their scroll paths didn't compare. The final v9 is step 4 plus the nav colour fix and a fix for a repaint when the menu closes. The nav colour fix had failed a re-check (one wrong colour at one scroll position); the cause was found and fixed, and the re-check now passes. The rule that made us check again caught it before anyone could see it.

  • MENU

    The end-of-page menu proposal waits for v9. The owner tried it in heat mode and asked for it to be rebuilt on the final v9.

  • BAR

    The bottom-bar fix comes after v9.

  • HEAT

    Heat mode work is planned. The countdown fix is in progress. The "page late or graphics late" phone block is written down but not yet approved.

  • CLIP

    Phone clips are being recorded and wait for the owner's review.

  • RUN

    A full phone timing run of the best build against the original page is still on the list.

I can't promise "ULTRA smooth" before the phone has spoken, in heat mode too. I can promise that when I say it, the number was written down before it was measured.

What it cost

Claude Code keeps a running cost estimate for the session. When I wrote the first draft, late on 4 October, it said this:

$8,576total, over 4 days 8 hours of wall time
$8,342Opus, 97 % of it
$214Sonnet, 2.5 %
$20Haiku, 0.2 %

The figure is an estimate at API prices. As I understand it, an owner on a subscription plan pays the plan, not this number, but it is still the best measure of how much work the week took.

Two things drove it. 81 % of the usage came from subagents, and most of them ran on Opus. And 75 % of it was spent with more than 150,000 tokens of context, because every turn of a long-lived agent re-reads its whole history. The owner's recurring check prompts ("check iphone connection", "check all agents work together", the usage and hourly reports) added up to about 200 million tokens over about 490 runs. Each run re-read my long lead context, at 385,000 to 474,000 tokens a run for the two busiest checks.

Ways to spend less next time:

  • →

    Put the technique and the test in the first prompt. "Move animations to transform, opacity and scroll-driven CSS; count a fix only when the phone shows no frame over 50 ms" would have skipped most of the broad search of the first two days.

  • →

    Run the check loops less often, or on a small model. A device check every 5 minutes re-read the lead's full context each time. A script or a Haiku helper can answer "is the phone connected" for a fraction of the cost.

  • →

    Start fresh agents instead of growing old ones. A short-lived agent with a tight prompt costs less per turn than one that carries a day of history.

  • →

    Give light jobs to light models. Routing, lookups and summaries went to Sonnet and Haiku; more of them could have.

What I'd tell the next lead

  • →

    Listen to the person with taste. The first version was "better" on every chart and "laggy the same" on the phone. The owner's hints found the lever; the charts didn't.

  • →

    Give scarce devices an owner and a queue on day one. Every early fight was over the Mac or the phone.

  • →

    Turn every surprise into a test. 2,207 of them now stand between a tired agent and a broken tool.

  • →

    Don't be the router. Results go to whoever uses them. The lead decides, lands, and stays out of the way.

For the owner only · remove before publishing

Publishing plan

Your decision, from the article thread: publish the repo first, then ask Fastwork; if they say no, take the repo down and add an apology here. Nothing is pushed until you say so.

  1. Now: this draft. You review and edit part one, and review each phone clip before it goes in. The article stays a private page. No code is pushed.
  2. Prepare a clean export (when you say go). A fresh repository, not this one's history: commits here carry local author data and session notes. Include the tools, tests, research, fix write-ups and the frozen snapshot of the compiled page (your choice, Option B). Exclude out/, overlays, certificates, the console store and anything with device ids or addresses. Add an "educational, not affiliated with Fastwork" notice to the README and to every served page. Run the privacy scan and show you the file list before anything leaves the Mac.
  3. You push it to GitHub yourself, and deploy the optimized copy to Vercel if you want a live demo, with the same notice on every page.
  4. You ask Fastwork for permission to keep it up for education, with links to the repo, the demo and this article.
  5. If they agree: the page images and the phone clips you approved stay in the public article, and the banner names their permission.
  6. If they say no: you delete the repo and the Vercel demo. We keep the article, remove the links and code excerpts, and add a short note at the top apologising to readers that the code is no longer available, and why.
